**Fix:** Contract 7.1 wording: "a merge is clean only when the result compiles and resolves, no check's outcome on the merge is worse than its outcome on each parent that defines it (`Pass` > `Undecided` > `Fail` > `Error`), and no interference appears that neither parent has." A geometric conflict becomes provenance-level: both sides modify, split or delete the same base entity, or one side's new entity intersects the other side's modified region. Symmetric-difference regions appear in review but do not block. Write "at or below the merge clearance". Add held-out merges with one-sided checks to `repo/merge`.

**Section:** KLN "Change management" (D-KLN-28), Rust API (`ChangeOrder`)
**Problem:** Approvals sign a record that names the head `ChangeId` and the CI report's `ObjectId`. A rebase changes the `ChangeId`, and a CI re-run changes the report (timings, workers, costs), so either voids approvals of identical content. That contradicts KLN's own rule that a rebase resets approvals "only if its evaluated content changes". With R3-01, a refactor voids them too.
**Evidence:** KLN: "A signature signs the order record, which names the head `ChangeId`, the evaluated `ItemDefinition`s and the CI report `ObjectId`"; `pub head: ChangeId, // the exact content approvals sign`; "the second must rebase onto the first, which resets its approvals only if its evaluated content changes".
**Fix:** Contract 5 defines `ApprovalSubject { base revisions, ItemDefinition GeometryIds with PMI, check-verdict digest (check id, verdict, fidelity, class, value, limit), effectivity, evidence record ids }`. Approvals sign its `ObjectId`; the `ChangeId` and the full CI report are unsigned provenance. A rebase or CI re-run keeps approvals exactly when the subject is unchanged. MFG's program approvals and AGT's Act plans keep their own subjects.

**Section:** CONTRACT 2 (External input), 7.1 (Hardware CI); KLN "Hardware CI runner" (D-KLN-35)
**Problem:** The contract makes a physical measurement an External input "pinned in `ingot.lock`", but hardware CI produces measurements automatically and keys them by the inputs they tested. Neither text says which measurement a check reads. A check's outcome for a fixed Change therefore depends on when it is evaluated, and a release cannot reproduce it.
**Evidence:** Contract 2: an External input includes "a machine reading, a physical measurement ... pinned in `ingot.lock`". KLN: "A measurement record is keyed by the check, the `ObjectId`s of the design inputs it tested, the rig and the run".
**Fix:** Contract 2 defines two pin modes. Lockfile pins cover translations, offers, catalog data and regulation packages, refreshed explicitly. Evidence pins cover measurement records, addressed by check id and the tested inputs' `GeometryId`s (R3-01). An evaluation reads the newest valid evidence record and stores its `ObjectId` in the `CheckOutcome`. Releases and approvals pin the evidence ids they cite, as 7.3 does for External Op results.

**Section:** CONTRACT 6 and 14 (variant ruling); KLN "Variants and the 150% BOM" (D-KLN-27); ELX "Variants" (D-ELX-4)
**Problem:** The ruling removed `options` and `when`, but the 150% BOM needs a static account of which Instances exist under which option values, and no tab now provides it. With plain `if` and `match`, an Instance's existence can depend on computed geometry. ELX's "every declared variant builds" enumerates configurations, which KLN rejects as exponential.
**Evidence:** KLN: "The Ingot compiler enforces that whether an Instance exists depends only on options and constants ... Kiln can then evaluate assembly structure with options as symbolic values". Contract 6: "variants are enum or record parameters selected with `if` and `match`". ING's Interfaces provide no such analysis.
**Fix:** ING adds an attribute, not a keyword: `#[configuration]` on enum or record parameters of an assembly feature. The compiler marks γ-regions whose conditions depend only on configuration parameters and constants as variant regions; Instances created inside them carry the region's condition. Creating an Instance under a condition that depends on computed values is a compile error. Kiln computes the 150% BOM by abstract interpretation of the IIR with configuration parameters symbolic, and SAT checks replace enumeration. ELX's CI builds only the configurations its policy lists.

**Section:** CONTRACT 7.1 (Kiln: reverse traversal, `Differentiable`, step checkpoints); KLN (whole tab); FLX "Adjoints for steady and transient problems"
**Problem:** The contract gives Kiln reverse traversal for adjoints, a `Differentiable` registration extension and step-keyed checkpoints, and ING and FLX depend on them. KLN specifies none of them, and section 14 lists no KLN edit. `OpImpl` has no tangent or adjoint methods while FLX writes its own over `OpCtx`, and the CAS has no retention class for checkpoints, which FLX requires.
**Evidence:** KLN contains no "Differentiable", "reverse traversal" or "retention class". Contract 7.1: "Reverse traversal for adjoints, a `Differentiable` registration extension and checkpoints keyed by step". ING: "`grad` over many parameters uses Kiln's reverse traversal of the Op graph". FLX: `fn tangent(..., ctx: &mut OpCtx)` and `fn adjoint(...)`; FLX requires "retention classes for checkpoints, intermediates and results".
**Fix:** KLN adds a "Derivatives" section. It defines `trait Differentiable: OpImpl { fn tangent(...); fn adjoint(...); }` in `base`, reverse traversal of the recorded dependency graph from a scalar goal, and checkpoints keyed by (`OpKey`, step) in a `Checkpoint` retention class that eviction drops first. Its oracle is a Taylor test of a three-Op chain. Add the edit to section 14.

**Section:** CONTRACT 7.1 (trusted builders); KLN "Distributed and remote evaluation" (D-KLN-9)
**Problem:** "Only trusted builders write the shared cache" trusts the machine, not the code it ran. CI runners evaluate untrusted agent Proposals and third-party Wasm, so a sandbox escape there produces a valid attestation for any key. Spot re-execution of 1% of hits rarely catches a targeted poisoning, and the global public domain that all tenants share has no named writer.
**Evidence:** KLN: "Only trusted builders write the shared result cache: CI runners and the organization's workers"; "Kiln continuously re-executes 1% of shared cache hits"; "values whose inputs are all public ... live in one global public domain that every tenant shares". KLN open question 1 asks whether release citations should be re-executed.
**Fix:** Contract 7.1: "Attestations from jobs that ran untrusted code (agent or external branches) are scoped to that Proposal until merge; results cited by a release or a protected merge are recomputed on a second, independent worker before signing; only the registry's reproducible builders write the global public domain." Signing keys are per job and held outside the sandboxed process, and the host, not the guest, computes output `ObjectId`s.

**Section:** KLN "Cancellation", "Sources of nondeterminism and their controls", "Requirements on the Platform tab"
**Problem:** KLN contradicts contract 7.4 and D-PLT-22 in three places: it cancels Wasm components with epoch interruption, it inserts NaN canonicalization at load time in browsers, and it relies on Cranelift's NaN switch natively, which D-PLT-22 rejects. Section 14 lists none of these as KLN edits. Cancellation also needs a mechanism that browsers support, and they have neither epochs nor engine fuel.
**Evidence:** KLN: "Wasm components are interrupted by Wasmtime epoch interruption"; "fuel for limits and epochs for cancellation"; "on browser engines ... Crucible's Wasm component loader inserts the same canonicalization". Contract 7.4: "epoch interruption is never used"; "Hosts execute only determinized binaries". D-PLT-22: "Wasmtime's epoch interruption is never used".
**Fix:** The determinizer's injected fuel check also reads a host-provided cancellation word in shared memory. Where no shared memory exists (single-threaded browser builds), the check yields to the host every fixed number of fuel units, and the host resumes or drops the call. Cancellation then behaves identically in Wasmtime, Pulley and browsers and lands only at fuel-check points. KLN deletes the epoch and load-time text and points to 7.4. Add these to section 14's KLN edits.

**Section:** KLN "Repository API"; ECO "API methods that ECO adds"; CONTRACT 7.6
**Problem:** KLN invents a ninth method group, "Govern", and makes `release.create` a direct method although a release is an Act. ECO lists `registry.yank` and `archive.export`, which 7.6 names as Acts, as plain methods. Method names follow three schemes (`read.tree`, `repo.undo`, `change_order.approve`). A release could then need two different approvals: change-order signatures and the Act's plan approval.
**Evidence:** KLN: "`change_order.approve(id, meaning, reauth)`, `release.create(order)`, `deviation.grant` | Govern". ECO: "`registry.yank`, `registry.deprecate` | Publisher-only status changes"; "`archive.export`, `archive.import`". Contract 7.6: "publish, yank and export are Acts"; glossary: Act includes "release".
**Fix:** Every method is `<group>.<name>` in the eight groups. Release, yank, export and deviation grants become Act classes. `act.prepare` produces the release plan, and the change order's approvals are the Approvals of that plan's digest, so one approval serves both. `policy.propose` becomes `propose.policy`, `repo.merge_preview` becomes `compare.merge_preview`, and `repo.undo` becomes `edit.undo`.

**Section:** KLN "Events and webhooks" (D-KLN-34); ECO "Events and webhooks" (D-ECO-12)
**Problem:** Two tabs specify the event envelope and webhook signing, and they contradict each other. KLN signs with HMAC-SHA-256 and defines its own envelope; ECO adopts CloudEvents and Standard Webhooks, signs with Ed25519 and rejects HMAC-only signing.
**Evidence:** KLN: "Each webhook request carries an HMAC-SHA-256 signature over the timestamp and body"; "An event envelope holds an id, type, organization, repository, subject id, server time, a per-repository sequence number". ECO D-ECO-12: "signed with Ed25519 (`v1a`) by default ... *Rejected:* ... HMAC-only signing (every receiver holds a secret that can forge events)".
**Fix:** ECO owns envelope, delivery and signing. KLN keeps only its repository and lifecycle event types, carries the per-repository sequence number as a CloudEvents extension attribute, and points to D-ECO-12.

**Section:** FLX "Co-simulation over FMI 3.0 and SSP"; ELX "Co-simulation over FMI and SSP" (D-ELX-17)
**Problem:** FMU import and export, master algorithms and SSP are specified twice, with different phases (FLX 3, ELX 4), different mappings and different oracles. FLX turns FMU variables into Fields; ELX makes an FMU a `Circuit` element.
**Evidence:** FLX rows "Import FMU (Co-Simulation)" through "Master algorithm", phase 3. ELX rows "FMU import (CS, ME, SE)" through "SSP", phase 4, plus D-ELX-17.
**Fix:** FLX owns the FMI and SSP runtime (import, export, master algorithms, Model Exchange integration) as External Ops and Flux operations in phase 3. ELX keeps two rows: an FMU instance is a `Network` element whose ports come from its model description, and FMI-LS-BUS. ECO keeps packaging (FMI-LS-WASM). ELX's section becomes a pointer.

**Section:** MFG "Electronics manufacturing handoff" (D-MFG-16); ELX "Fabrication and assembly outputs"
**Problem:** Both tabs specify board fabrication and assembly outputs (Gerber, drill, IPC-2581, ODB++, pick-and-place), and they disagree. MFG calls Gerber revision 2024.05 current, which is outdated. MFG also routes ODB++ through a "plugin", a term the contract replaces with external tools.
**Evidence:** MFG: "its specification is current (revision 2024.05)". ELX: "Gerber Layer Format Specification, revision 2026.05". Ucamco lists "Gerber Layer Format Specification - Revision 2026.05", dated 19/05/2026 (https://www.ucamco.com/en/gerber/downloads). Contract 7.7: licensed translators "run as external tools outside evaluation".
**Fix:** One owner each. MFG owns the factory handoff (package choice, panelization, DFM and DFA, test), ELX owns the board model it serializes, and ECO owns the `io/` writers. ELX's output table moves to MFG. Update MFG to revision 2026.05 and call ODB++ a "licensed external tool".

**Section:** CONTRACT 4 and 7.4 (`crucible:ops`); ECO "First-party WIT packages"; ING "Rules for Rust features"
**Problem:** The contract names the host interface `crucible:ops`, but ECO's WIT catalog has no such package and puts Anvil's operations at `crucible:geom/ops`. ING follows ECO, and no interface exposes Flux operations, which ELX's placer needs. Calling `crucible:ops` an "interface" also blurs WIT's distinction between packages and interfaces.
**Evidence:** Contract 7.4: "they may import `crucible:ops`"; ruling ELX-7: "Accepted: `crucible:ops`". ECO: "`crucible:geom` | `types` ..., `ops` (generated from Anvil's operation catalog)", with no Flux `ops`. ELX requires a "2D FFT Poisson solve and batched gradient kernels for the placer" callable from Wasm components.
**Fix:** Use one package, `crucible:ops`, with one generated interface per catalog: `crucible:ops/anvil` and `crucible:ops/flux`. ECO removes `ops` from `crucible:geom`; contract 4 and 7.4 say "the WIT package `crucible:ops`"; ING and ELX use those names.

**Section:** CONTRACT 5 and 12 (`base`); KLN Rust API; PLT Rust API (`runtime`); AGT "Rate, cost and size limits"
**Problem:** `kiln` sits in the engine core but needs types owned by layers above it: `Budget` and priority classes from AGT's `api`, `PrincipalId`, and residency decisions from `repo::policy`. Two operation-context types coexist (`OpCx` in the contract and KLN, `OpCtx` in PLT, FLX and ING's SDK). `Priority` and `Durability` each name two different concepts.
**Evidence:** KLN: `pub budget: Budget` is "the type the agents tab defines"; `pub enum Priority { Interactive, Agent, Ci, Batch }`; "Placement respects labels"; policy evaluation lives in "a `repo::policy` module". PLT: `pub enum Priority { Interactive, Background }`, `pub enum Durability` (write durability), `pub struct OpCtx<'a>`. KLN: `pub enum Durability { Low, Medium, High }`. AGT: `pub money: Option<Money>`, against the contract's `Money<C>`.
**Fix:** Contract 5 adds to `base`: `PrincipalId`, `Budget`, `PriorityClass`, `Labels`, `ResultStatus`, `CheckOutcome`, and a `PlacementPolicy` trait that `repo::policy` implements and Kiln calls. It also adds a Rust `Money { amount: Decimal, currency: Currency }` that std's `Money<C>` maps to. One `OpCx` in `base` wraps PLT's runtime handles. PLT renames its `Priority` to `PoolLane` and its `Durability` to `WriteDurability`.

**Section:** ING worked example 2; ELX "Catalog-part selection" (D-ELX-3)
**Problem:** ING says a catalog query in a feature body re-resolves when its argument changes and that "the chosen part is pinned in the lockfile". ELX says selections resolve only when the lockfile is updated and builds read the pinned answer. If the answer is pinned, changing `shaft_d` cannot re-resolve without running `update`. ELX also calls a catalog selection a `Query`, which is the core type for geometric selection.
**Evidence:** ING: "`bearing_62xx(bore: p.shaft_d)?  // catalog query; the chosen part is pinned in the lockfile`" and "Changing `shaft_d` re-resolves the bearing". D-ELX-3: "a parametric selection, which is a `Query` over the catalog. Selections resolve when the lockfile is created or updated ... builds read the pinned result". Contract 2: a catalog part's definition is a data package, and its offers are External inputs.
**Fix:** A selection is a pure function over pinned definition packages, plus pinned offer External inputs when it ranks by price or stock. It re-resolves whenever its arguments change. `crucible update parts` refreshes only the data pins, and its diff lists substitutions. Name the type `CatalogSelection`, and correct ING's comment.

**Section:** CONTRACT 5 (`Quantity<D>`, ruling ING-7); ING "Dimensions" (D-ING-3)
**Problem:** Making angle a base dimension while keeping torque in N·m leaves the basic laws of rotation ill-typed: power τω, work τθ, τ = Iα and kinetic energy ½Iω² each carry stray radians. ω = √(k/I) yields A^(−1/2)·T⁻¹, which rational exponents accept without complaint. Moment of inertia and rotational stiffness have no stated convention, and for a rotational `Network` port, across times through is not a power.
**Evidence:** With A a base dimension and torque M·L²·T⁻²: τω = M·L²·T⁻³·A; with I = kg·m², ½Iω² = M·L²·T⁻²·A²; k = τ/θ = M·L²·T⁻²·A⁻¹, so k/I = T⁻²·A⁻¹. mp-units' strong angular system, the consistent alternative, uses torque in J·rad⁻¹ and moment of inertia in kg·m²·rad⁻² (https://mpusz.github.io/mp-units/latest/users_guide/systems/strong_angular_system/). ELX: a port type declares "its across and through quantities as `Quantity` dimensions".
**Fix:** Choose one consistent system in phase 0 and publish it as a std table. Recommended: keep A as a base dimension and adopt the strong system for derived rotational kinds: `Torque` = J/rad, `MomentOfInertia` = kg·m²/rad², `RotationalStiffness` = J/rad². Named units keep datasheet literals short (for example, `Nm` defined as N·m/rad, while `[N*m]` stays energy). Each `Network` port type declares its power expression, and the compiler checks that it is a power. ING-O-4 gains 50 textbook rotational formulas that must type-check without casts.

**Section:** ING "`Tol<T>`", "Arithmetic on tolerances" (D-ING-4, D-ING-5)
**Problem:** The `Tol<T>` record (nominal, lower, upper, basis, form) cannot hold an affine form, so `bore - shaft` has no representation. "One symbol per site" also conflates a specification with a characteristic. `let spec = 2mm ± 0.05mm` passed to two different Parts gives both spacers one noise symbol, so a code-level stack that uses them with opposite signs reports zero variation, which is unconservative.
**Evidence:** ING: `pub record Tol<T: Toleranceable> { nominal, lower, upper, basis, form }`; "a computed `Tol` is an affine form: a center plus one coefficient per symbol"; "A `Tol` value written in code has one symbol per site, so reusing the value models one characteristic"; "`t.independent(key)` makes an explicit independent copy".
**Fix:** Make `Tol<T>` opaque, with `nominal`, `center`, `terms: [(Symbol, T::Delta)]`, `remainder` and `form`; `lower` and `upper` become methods. When a value is forwarded into a Part, key its symbol by (tolerance site, realizing Part or Instance path), so separate parts vary independently by default; code-level stacks keep site identity. New lint `ING9301`: one symbol appears with both signs in one expression; suggest `.independent()`.

**Section:** ING "Inference" (coercions), "Approximate values as inputs", "Sketches and constraints" (D-ING-9), open question 11
**Problem:** Numbers come in four flavors (`T`, `Tol<T>`, `Approx<T>`, `Expr<T>`), each lifted by its own rule at its own call positions, and those rules break the tab's own examples. `rect` is a `fn`, and plain `fn` parameters "never coerce", so the motivating `rect(other.edge(longest).length(), 10mm)` does not compile. D-ING-9's claim that "any pure Ingot function works on symbolic values" fails for any `fn` declared over `Length`, since `Expr<Length>` is not `Length`.
**Evidence:** ING: coercion 5 applies "at feature and operation argument positions only"; "Plain `fn` parameters never coerce"; open question 11: std helpers "(`rect`, `fit`) are `fn`"; D-ING-9: "any pure Ingot function works on symbolic values without a restricted dialect".
**Fix:** One mechanism: a `Scalar<D>` trait implemented by `Quantity<D>`, `Tol`, `Approx` and `Expr`, with arithmetic and std math generic over it. A parameter written `Length` accepts any `Scalar<L>` at every call position, `fn` and `feature` alike, with fixed semantics per flavor: nominal plus forwarding for `Tol`, guaranteed bounds only for `Approx`, staging for `Expr`. A parameter that must be exact is written `Exact<Length>`. Restate D-ING-9 to match.

**Section:** ING "Lossless syntax tree" (block table), D-ING-18; KLN "CRDT over the syntax tree"
**Problem:** The live document's block tree is authoritative, but the grammar is specified only for whole files. When a block's text stops parsing (say, an unbalanced brace from a concurrent edit), a file-level parser re-associates the blocks after it. "The last good result for that block" then has no defined meaning, and the parse can disagree with the CRDT's tree.
**Evidence:** ING: "Statement | The statement's text up to its first nested block ... | Arms ... | Text after the last arm"; the parser "wraps malformed input in `ERROR` nodes". KLN: "Concurrent edits can leave a block that does not parse ... the UI shows the last good result for that block".
**Fix:** ING specifies block-local parsing. Each block kind parses as head ⧺ arm holes ⧺ tail under its own production, and delimiters belong to the head and tail of the arm they open and close. An error stays inside its block and never consumes sibling bytes. Two oracles: parse(concat(tree)) reproduces the tree whenever every block parses, and a failed block keeps its kind and position.

**Section:** ING "The deterministic Wasm subset" (Memory), "Values and memory", "Resource limits"; KLN "Memory management and eviction"
**Problem:** Each feature call runs in its own instance whose module "declares its maximum memory, and the host reserves it"; the default per-call limit is 1 GiB, and KLN's browser budget is 2 GiB. Suspended parent calls stay alive while their children run, so as specified a browser holds about two live feature calls. A std feature that calls a std feature that calls a third would then abort.
**Evidence:** ING: "Memory | Semantic bytes ... | 1 GiB"; "The module declares its maximum memory, and the host reserves it in its memory budget before instantiation"; "Each feature call runs in a fresh instance drawn from a pool". KLN: "2 GiB in browsers".
**Fix:** Reserve semantic memory as it is used, not the declared maximum. Run suspended feature calls as state machines in one instance per worker, each with its own allocator region and fuel and depth counters. Isolation then comes from the compiler (no mutable globals) and the allocator. Add a browser benchmark: 500 concurrently suspended feature calls fit within 2 GiB.

**Section:** ANV "Persistence and versioning"; KLN "Memoization, verification and backdating" (D-KLN-5), "Memory management and eviction"
**Problem:** The Body encoding normalizes −0.0 to +0.0, while Kiln's in-memory equality treats them as different and Kiln reloads evicted and warm-start values from that encoding. A value read from memory and the same value reloaded can differ in the sign of zero. That changes `atan2`, `copysign`, `1/x` and sign tests downstream, so results depend on eviction and cache state.
**Evidence:** ANV: "IEEE binary64 floats with −0.0 normalized to +0.0". KLN: "buffer contents bitwise (so `-0.0` and `+0.0` differ ...)"; "if the value is demanded again, Kiln reloads it from the local CAS by `ObjectId`"; "Large buffers ... are memory-mapped from the local CAS".
**Fix:** Canonicalize at the operation boundary: every `OpOutputs` value is already canonical, so decode(encode(v)) equals v bit for bit. New oracle `kiln/roundtrip`: every Op output, fed once from memory and once reloaded through each dependent, gives identical results.

**Section:** UIX "Localization and units", Interfaces (`render_snapshot`); AGT "Rendered views and Field overlays" (D-AGT-9)
**Problem:** Snapshots are content-addressed results of `render_snapshot(ViewState, size)` and serve as Proposal evidence and benchmark grading. Their legends and labels depend on locale ("4,5 mm in German"), theme, display units, bundled fonts and the renderer version, and none of these is in `ViewState` or the call. Two agents' snapshots of one state can differ, and a cached snapshot can show another user's locale or an older renderer.
**Evidence:** UIX: `render_snapshot(ViewState, size) -> CasRef<Image>`, "deterministic per platform class on the CPU path"; "Display follows the locale (4,5 mm in German)". Contract 5: `ViewState` holds "camera, visibility, sections and Field displays". D-AGT-9: snapshots "must be reproducible".
**Fix:** Add a `RenderProfile` (locale, theme, display units, font package pins, renderer behavior version) to the snapshot key. Proposals and benchmarks use one fixed review profile (`en`, SI with millimetres, light theme), so evidence is reproducible.

**Section:** CONTRACT 11 (skeleton); ING "Capability catalog"; UIX "Capability catalog"; KLN capability tables; MEC "Sketching contract", "Assembly oracles and phases", "Tolerancing contract", "Drawing and MBD oracles"; ELX "Layout capability catalog"
**Problem:** Section 11 demands "for every capability: what it does, its contract, failure behavior, oracle and phase" but gives that information no place. The tabs invented four layouts: one catalog section (ING, UIX), a table per section (KLN), contract and oracle subsections scattered through the design (MEC, ELX), or none. Phases and oracles are then stated two or three times.
**Evidence:** UIX "Capability catalog" (1,326 words) beside "Oracles" (1,027); KLN has eight capability tables plus "Oracles"; MEC has four contract or oracle subsections inside design sections.
**Fix:** Amend section 11: each design section ends with one table (Capability · Contract · Failure · Oracle id · Phase); `## Oracles` lists each oracle once (id · verifies · pass criterion) with no phase column; `## Phasing` lists gate contributions only. Separate catalog sections go.

**Section:** PLT "Numerical determinism"; KLN "Determinism policy"; FLX "Determinism"; ANV "Determinism rules"; ECO "Determinism contract"; ING "Determinism guarantees"
**Problem:** Six tabs each list the sources of nondeterminism and their controls, about 4,000 words in all, against "Say it once". The tables already drift, as R3-21's NaN and loader text shows.
**Evidence:** KLN "Sources of nondeterminism and their controls" (1,203 words); PLT "Sources of divergence and their controls" (547); FLX "Determinism" (733); ANV "Determinism rules" (523); ECO "Determinism contract" (921); ING's "Determinism guarantees" table.
**Fix:** PLT owns the single mechanism table, KLN owns the policy (grades and their acceptance), and contract 7.3 and 7.4 own the rules. Each engine tab and ECO keeps at most 150 words of operation-specific rules plus a pointer. This saves about 3,000 words.

**Section:** ANV "Operations catalog", "Build, reuse or avoid", naming worked examples, "GPU strategy and freedom to operate", "Rust API", "Mesh representation", "Implicit representation"
**Problem:** At 31,956 words, Anvil is 60% over its 20,000-word cap. Its prose re-explains algorithms that earlier sections specify, and several decisions are argued twice.
**Evidence:** Operations catalog 7,104 words, including "Booleans" (465) plus "Booleans for every representation pair" (491) and "Blends" (778). "Build, reuse or avoid" (705) restates D-ANV-23 and the State of the art table; the four naming worked examples take 673; "GPU strategy and freedom to operate" (612) restates D-ANV-17; Rust API 1,334.
**Fix:** Cut the Operations catalog to about 3,500 words, one table per family (operation · inputs → outputs · failure · oracle · phase), and merge the two Boolean sections. "Build, reuse or avoid" becomes a column of the State of the art table. Keep worked example 1 only, and cut "GPU strategy" to 200 words with the patent analysis moved to the freedom-to-operate memo. Rust API to 500 words (`Body`, `EntityId`, `ErrorBound`, one operation call); Mesh to 1,400 and Implicit to 1,500. Result: about 19,500 words with every decision, oracle and source kept.

**Section:** ING "Comparison with existing languages", "Capability catalog", "Compilation strategy", "Worked examples", "Tooling", "Rust features", "Calling Wasm components", "Contract change requests"
**Problem:** At 30,209 words, Ingot is 51% over its 20,000-word cap. Several sections restate one another.
**Evidence:** "What Ingot adopts" and "What Ingot rejects" restate the comparison table and the decisions' Rejected clauses. "Options compared" restates D-ING-13, and "Identical behavior everywhere" repeats Platform notes. Worked example 1 repeats the canonical example's constructs, and example 5 repeats "Rust features". The capability catalog repeats Oracles and Phasing, and all ten CCRs are now ruled.
**Fix:** Delete the adopt and reject tables and keep a ten-row comparison inside State of the art. Delete "Options compared" (D-ING-13 holds it) and fold "Identical behavior everywhere" into Platform notes. Keep worked examples 2 to 4 and only the Ingot half of 5. Merge "Rust features" with "Calling Wasm components" (about 800 words) and compress Tooling (debugger, REPL, tests, benchmarks) into one table. Replace the CCR list with any new requests. Result: about 19,800 words.

**Section:** KLN "Scope and terms", "Determinism policy", capability tables, "Threat model", "Software supply chain", "Events and webhooks", "Identical behavior on every Tier 1 platform", "Rust API"; lead
**Problem:** At 25,443 words, KLN is 7,400 over the cap. It redefines contract terms, carries eight capability tables beside Oracles and repeats other tabs' threat and supply-chain material. Its lead claims "identical bits on every Tier 1 machine", which holds only for `Portable` results.
**Evidence:** "Scope and terms" (390 words) redefines `ObjectId`, `OpKey`, node, `Fidelity` and Change. "Sources of nondeterminism" takes 1,203 words (R3-37). The threat rows on prompt injection, exfiltration and the lethal trifecta repeat AGT's. "Identical behavior on every Tier 1 platform" (296) repeats contract 9, and the Rust API runs 1,367.
**Fix:** Cut "Scope and terms" to 150 words and Determinism policy to 900 (grades and acceptance only). Fold the capability tables into R3-36's layout. Agent threats stay in AGT and supply chain in ECO, each with a one-line pointer. Delete "Identical behavior" and "Requirements on the Platform tab", and cut the Rust API to 600 words (`OpImpl`, `OpCx`, `ObjectId`, `Change`, `MergeDriver`). Lead: "with identical bits within each platform class". Result: about 17,800 words.

**Section:** UIX "Capability catalog", "Oracles", "Renderer", "State of the art", "Design system and visual language", "Interface principles", "Platforms and devices", "Platform notes"
**Problem:** At 25,578 words, UIX is 7,600 over the cap. It has 19 design sections, a capability catalog that duplicates Oracles and Phasing, and two platform sections.
**Evidence:** "Capability catalog" (1,326 words) plus "Oracles" (1,027); "Renderer" 3,820; "Color tokens" 526; "Interface principles" (306) restates contract 3 and 10; "Platforms and devices" (550) beside "Platform notes" (496).

**Section:** CONTRACT §2 (Act); MFG Approval and machine safety, Printer profiles, 3MF and machine connectivity, Machine and MES connectivity, Platform notes; AGT Irreversible real-world actions, Phasing; KLN Hardware CI runner.
**Problem:** No tab separates moving data to a device from starting motion, heat or energy, and none forbids Crucible from starting a machine remotely. MFG ships printer "start" and OPC UA job writes as plain "`api` actions" in phases 1 to 3, while AGT's Act machinery for `send_to_machine` arrives only in phase 2 and lets the agent commit after a remote approval reached "through the review UI and Tier 2 notifications". KLN lets agent branches run `unattended_safe` rigs although MFG requires a person to approve every program, and the tabs disagree on who may transfer (MFG: never agents; AGT: agents prepare and commit) and on Act names (`transfer_program`, `start_build` against `send_to_machine`).
**Evidence:** MFG: "Printer connectivity | Send, start, pause, cancel, monitor through plugins (OctoPrint, Moonraker, PrusaLink, vendor APIs, MTConnect, OPC UA) as `api` actions | … | 1"; D-MFG-4 "agents can neither approve nor transfer programs"; OPC UA adapter "production jobs … are written only where allowed"; "Shop-floor approval requires a Tier 1 client or a Tier 2 client with an authenticated approval key". AGT: CAM programmer role holds `send_to_machine`; phase 1 has only the `release` Act. KLN: "Runs requested from agent branches use only rigs marked `unattended_safe`". OPC 10031-4 ISA-95 Job Control, which OPC 40001-3 Machinery Job Management (1.0.1, 2024-05-01) builds on, lists `Start`, `StoreAndStart`, `Resume` and `RevokeStart` methods on the job-order receiver (https://reference.opcfoundation.org/ISA95JOBCONTROL/v200/docs/6.3; https://reference.opcfoundation.org/Machinery/Jobs/v100/docs/). ISO 10218-1:2025 and ISO 10218-2:2025 replaced the 2011 robot safety editions (https://www.iso.org/standard/73933.html; https://www.iso.org/standard/73934.html).
**Fix:** Contract §2, Act row, append: "Acts with a physical effect are transfer Acts (send an NC program, print job or robot program to a device) or start Acts. Crucible never issues cycle start, resume, jog, `Start` or `StoreAndStart` to machine tools, robots, lasers, presses or furnaces; a person starts them at the device. `start_print` exists only for printers whose profile declares thermal-runaway protection and enclosure or smoke detection, and needs an Approval of the job digest plus an on-site confirmation that the build plate is clear, given on the printer or with a site-bound key at the gateway. A Tier 2 or remote approval never gives the on-site confirmation." MFG and AGT adopt one list: `send_to_machine`, `send_print_job`, `start_print`, `send_robot_program`, `store_machine_job` (OPC UA `Store` only); machine data collection is a Read. The OPC UA adapter's capability set excludes `Start`, `StoreAndStart`, `Resume` and `RevokeStart`. Rewrite D-MFG-4: "Agents may prepare transfer Acts; the server executes them only after a human Approval; no agent can give an on-site confirmation." KLN: `unattended_safe` is a signed site policy, never self-declared by a runner and never granted to machine tools, robots or lasers; agent-branch runs still need an Approval of the program digest. MFG robot offline programming: posted robot programs are proved first in the robot's manual reduced-speed mode and never alter the controller's safety configuration (safety-rated zones, speed limits); the robot safety data package cites the 2025 editions above. AGT moves `send_to_machine`, `send_print_job` and `start_print` to phase 1, because MFG and KLN ship those effects in phase 1.

**Section:** Machine models; Controllers and post-processors; Material removal and machine collision simulation; Oracles.
**Problem:** Collision verification checks the toolpath, not how the control moves between programmed points. The `Controller` record has no fields for rapid traverse interpolation (straight line or each axis at its own rate), rotary rapid direction and unwinding, TCP state during rapids and tool changes, reference-return intermediate points, canned-cycle retract planes, or cutter-compensation entry and look-ahead. Those are where verified programs crash in practice, so the claim that rapids are checked "with the same rigor as cuts" is unsafe as specified.
**Evidence:** MFG: `controller: Controller, // dialect, options, capability flags`; "The model describes nominal kinematics only."; "Rapid-move safety | Rapids checked against stock and fixture with the same rigor as cuts | `Collision` | As above | 1". ISO 6983-1 defines program format and address words (https://www.iso.org/standard/34608.html); positioning (G00) fixes the end point, and the path between points is control-specific [unverified per control; a Fanuc parameter, for example, selects linear or non-linear positioning]. Nothing in the seeded crash corpus specification plants controller-semantics crashes.
**Fix:** Add `MotionSemantics` to `Controller`: `rapid: Linear | PerAxis { rates }`, `rotary_rapid: Shortest | Directional | Unwind`, `tcp_in_rapid: Bool`, `reference_return: ViaIntermediate`, `cycle_retract: { initial_plane, r_plane }`, `cutter_comp: { lookahead_blocks, entry_rule }`, `tool_change_envelope: Body`. Collision simulation and the independent re-interpreter both execute the posted NC text under these semantics, never the pre-post toolpath. Where a semantic is undeclared, the simulator sweeps a conservative envelope (for a rapid, the joint-space box between the endpoints) and reports `Unsupported` instead of passing. Posts get a rule: convert G0 to G1 at a declared rapid-equivalent feed wherever the conservative envelope comes closer to stock or fixture than the declared clearance. Add to the crash corpus: dog-leg rapids through clamps, rotary unwinding through the fixture, reference return through the part, wrong retract plane over a clamp, cutter-compensation entry gouge, tool change inside the work envelope. Gate: zero false negatives on that corpus for each controller family before its post ships.

**Section:** ELX Writing a circuit; State of the art (connectivity capture); KLN Merge (D-KLN-21).
**Problem:** Because `connect` accumulates idempotently as a set union, two branches that each attach the same pin to a different net merge without textual conflict and silently short the two nets. None of KLN's five merge conditions catches it: the merged program compiles, Queries resolve, ERC passes unless pin types or voltage domains clash, and DRC follows the merged netlist, so the short becomes the design. ELX's merge target scores this case as a success.
**Evidence:** ELX: "`connect` statements accumulate into one value, and connecting the same pins twice is idempotent."; State of the art target "Scripted concurrent-edit branch pairs, target 100% merged without manual conflict when edits touch different nets". KLN D-KLN-21: merge succeeds when the design "compiles, resolves, passes every check that both parents passed, and shows no new geometric overlap or interference". Example: branch A adds `connect(u1.pin("PA5"), led_net)`, branch B adds `connect(u1.pin("PA5"), button_net)`; the merge joins both nets through PA5.
**Fix:** KLN adds a sixth merge condition: "Connectivity. The driver computes the net partition (pins per net) of base, both sides and merge. A merged net that unions nets that are distinct in the base and in each side is `Conflict::NetMerge`, naming the pins, both nets and both Changes. Net renames are matched by provenance, not by name." ELX adds an ERC rule that two named nets join only through an explicit `tie(...)` element (R4-22). Replace the ELX target with "100% of net-merging branch pairs reported as conflicts; 100% of non-overlapping pairs merged clean". Apply the condition to harness `Circuit`s and `std::systems` interface connections too.

**Section:** UIX Modes; Extending the interface; Capability catalog; Migration from other CAD tools; ELX Interactive routing; What this tab requires (UIX row).
**Problem:** UIX hosts electronics only as Wasm panels that return element trees, may not draw pixels and get 2 ms of CPU per frame, yet ELX requires schematic and layout editors with push-and-shove routing at 16 ms per mouse move. A layered board canvas with net highlighting, ratsnest, DRC markers and a live router head cannot be built from stacks, grids and overlay glyphs inside 2 ms, and UIX has no Electronics mode, no electronics role and no Altium or KiCad key presets. As written, the board designer's daily tools have no owner.
**Evidence:** UIX: "Domain views from other tabs, such as the electronics board view …, use the same extension points as any third-party package."; panels "never draw pixels or ship shaders"; "Each panel gets 2 ms of CPU per frame."; modes are Design, Simulate, Manufacture and Review; presets "for SOLIDWORKS, Fusion, Onshape and Blender users". ELX: "Targets: under 16 ms per mouse-move update with up to 50 shoved items"; ELX requires "Schematic and layout editors writing `Schematic`, `Layout` and source edits; constraint manager view; waveform, Smith chart, eye diagram and timeline viewers".
**Fix:** UIX adds an Electronics mode (Schematic, Layout) and a public `crucible:ui/canvas2d` world any package may use, so principle 1 holds: a component submits retained 2D primitive buffers (lines, arcs, polygons, text, with layer ids and net ids) that the wgpu renderer draws with layer visibility, opacity, high-contrast and net-highlight modes, and hit-testing uses the same buffers. Tools that compute per pointer move (the router, placement drag with live DRC) run in the engine process on an interactive edit lane like Kiln's drag lane and stream head geometry each frame through `api`; the 2 ms budget applies to panel UI logic only. Specify the schematic canvas (symbols, wires, junctions, labels, sheet frames, cross-references), the layout canvas (layer stack, ratsnest, DRC markers, length-tuning meters) and the constraint-manager grid, with budgets equal to ELX's targets. Add Altium-like and KiCad-like presets and an electronics first-run role. Phase 3, with a UIX oracle that replays ELX's recorded routing sessions at 16 ms or less per update.

**Section:** MFG Approval and machine safety; Machine and MES connectivity (program transfer); Platform notes.
**Problem:** Approval binding ends where Crucible hands the file over. A control cannot verify a signature, operators routinely edit programs, offsets and feeds at the control, and the controller's actual tool lengths and work offsets decide whether the simulated program is the one that runs; none of this is captured. Large 3D and 5-axis programs on older controls also need drip-feed DNC, which arrives only in phase 3.
**Evidence:** MFG: "Program transfer | Released programs to controllers, bound to the approval hash: signed file export first, then DNC, OPC UA and vendor plugins | Hash mismatch blocks transfer | … | 1 (file export), 3 (DNC, OPC UA)"; "A wrong tool length in the machine or a mis-clamped part is outside what any software can see." MTConnect 2.5 Part 3 lists observation types `PROGRAM`, `PROGRAM_HEADER`, `PROGRAM_EDIT`, `PROGRAM_EDIT_NAME`, `ToolOffsets` and `WorkOffsets` (https://docs.mtconnect.org/MBSD_MTConnect_Part_3_2-5-0.pdf, contents).
**Fix:** (1) Posts write a header comment with item, program revision, release id and a short content hash; the gateway recomputes it on transfer and on read-back. (2) Pre-run verification: before enabling transfer, the gateway reads tool and work offset tables (MTConnect `ToolOffsets` and `WorkOffsets`, OPC UA, a vendor plugin, or operator entry against the setup sheet) and re-runs collision simulation with the actual gauge lengths and offsets; a mismatch beyond the setup-sheet tolerance blocks transfer with `MfgError::OffsetMismatch`. (3) Edit capture: the gateway watches `PROGRAM_EDIT` and the active program header, uploads edited programs (DNC receive) and opens a Proposal with the semantic NC diff against the release; parts made from an edited program get a deviation in the as-built record. (4) Move DNC transfer, including drip feed with XON/XOFF or RTS/CTS flow control, to phase 1 in the gateway. (5) Oracles: recorded edit sessions yield Proposals with exact diffs; a seeded offset-mismatch corpus is blocked 100%.

**Section:** MFG Tool libraries, Controllers and post-processors, What MFG provides; UIX Toolpath preview and playback, Modes.
**Problem:** Neither tab produces a setup sheet, the document every machinist runs from: tools with holder, stick-out, gauge length, T, H and D numbers and pocket; stock size and material; work offset location and probing instructions; clamping views; program names and cycle times. UIX shows toolpaths but no NC text, although MFG already keeps a `BlockMap` from blocks to toolpath points. A reference shop cannot run GP1 without these.
**Evidence:** 07-manufacturing.md contains no "setup sheet", "tool table" or "G54". UIX toolpath table covers toolpaths, tool and holder, stock, collisions and additive only. MFG: "Each `BlockMap` entry links a posted block to its workingstep, path parameter and content hash."
**Fix:** MFG adds `setup_sheet(program, template) -> Drawing` in phase 1, an Ingot drawing built from the `Program`, tool Assemblies and setup, so it diffs and releases with the program; templates are packages. Content: setup views with the WCS triad and dimensions from the work offset to datum features, fixture and clamp positions, stock definition, tool table (T, pocket, H, D, holder, stick-out, gauge length, flute length, expected life), workingstep list with tool, cycle time and Z extremes, and first-run notes (tool-length verification, reduced override) from MFG's safety text. UIX Manufacture mode adds an NC code panel with two-way highlighting through `BlockMap` (block, toolpath point, workingstep, design feature) and a setup-sheet preview. Oracle: every tool in the program appears once in the table, with gauge length equal to the tool Assembly's analytic stack-up.

**Section:** Core manufacturing types; Machine models; Fixture and jig design; Phasing.
**Problem:** A `Setup` holds one part Instance and one `datum: Transform`, and a `Program` holds one setup, so everyday setups cannot be expressed: two parts in a double vise, op 1 and op 2 in one vise and one program, a tombstone with eight work offsets, extended offsets, pallet changers. Fourth-axis indexing and rotary wrapping on vertical machining centers appear nowhere, and vises, modular fixtures, soft jaws and probing wait for phase 2 although GP1 needs workholding.
**Evidence:** MFG: `pub record Setup { machine, fixture, stock, part: Instance, datum: Transform }`; `pub record Program { setup: Setup, steps: [Workingstep] }`; "Modular fixtures … | 2", "Soft jaws and nests … | 2", "Probing … | 2"; "4-axis" appears only for wire EDM.
**Fix:** Replace with `Setup { machine, fixture: Assembly, stations: [Station] }`, `Station { part: Instance, stock: Body, wcs: WorkOffset }`, `WorkOffset { number: WcsId, frame: CoordSys }` (G54 to G59, extended and fixture offsets as the controller declares) and `Program { setups: [Setup], order: ByTool | ByStation }`. Add 4th-axis indexing (3+1) in phase 1 and rotary wrapping in phase 2, with A or B rotary kinematics in machine models. Move vise and modular-fixture catalog parts (jaw stroke, clamping force) and work-offset probing cycles to phase 1. Oracle: a tombstone corpus in which each station's toolpath is verified in its own WCS and posted offsets match the setup sheet.

**Section:** Controllers and post-processors.
**Problem:** Post tuning is the most frequent CAM customization in a shop, but logic that data cannot express needs Rust compiled to Wasm, which shop post editors will not write and which contradicts the contract's Ingot-first tier rule. There is no path from a shop's proven posts and programs (machine-builder M-codes, tool-change macros, safe-start blocks, probing macros) to Crucible posts.
**Evidence:** MFG: "Post extension hooks | Rust Wasm component hooks for logic that data cannot express | … | 2". Contract §4: "Use Ingot unless code needs more than about 10⁶ primitive steps per call, an existing codebase in another language, or a data structure Ingot cannot express efficiently".
**Fix:** Post hooks are Ingot functions over typed block events (`on_program_start`, `on_tool_change`, `on_wcs_change`, `on_rapid`, `on_cycle`, `on_program_end`) in phase 1; Rust Wasm hooks only for the contract's exceptions. Add post qualification against legacy output: the shop supplies a proven program from its current CAM for a reference part, and Crucible's semantic NC diff must show only differences on a declared list; the qualification record ships in the machine package. Machine packages carry machine-builder customizations (M-code map, tool-change macro, coolant variants, chip conveyor, spindle warm-up) as data. Oracle: per controller in the conformance corpus, the posted reference program equals the shop's proven program modulo the declared list.

**Section:** MFG Rust surface, Oracles; ECO Manufacturing and metrology, Migration from incumbent tools.
**Problem:** Shops hold thousands of proven NC programs from other CAM systems and from hand programming, and they need to verify them (backplot, material removal, machine collision) and keep them under revision control. MFG makes the NC interpreter oracle-only and offers no capability to simulate external NC, and ECO's migration lists no manufacturing data.
**Evidence:** MFG: `pub trait NcInterpreter { // independent implementation, used only by oracles`. ECO: G-code "W; R for verification"; "What can move" lists parts, assemblies, PMI, mates, metadata, drawings and PDM history only.
**Fix:** Add `verify_nc(nc: Asset, machine, setup, tools) -> (stock, collisions, gouges, cycle time, BlockMap)` in phase 1 on a product interpreter kept separate from the oracle interpreter, so the oracle stays independent. Legacy programs import as Items (kind `Program`, see R4-11) linked to part revision and machine, with the same approval and transfer path. ECO's migration table adds NC programs (verified, never converted to workingsteps), tool libraries (R4-10), post configurations (R4-08) and setup sheets as Assets. Oracle: hand-written and third-party-CAM programs with planted crashes, all detected.

**Section:** Tool libraries.
**Problem:** ISO 13399 import is necessary but is not how tool data reaches shops: vendors publish packaged catalogs (GTC packages built on ISO 13399, and DIN 4000 property lists [unverified]), shops keep libraries in their current CAM, and measured lengths come from presetters. Holders lack a full collision-body rule, there is no per-machine tool table, and tool-life tracking waits for phase 4.
**Evidence:** MFG: "ISO 13399 import | Vendor packages to Catalog parts … | 1"; "Shop library | A package of tool Assemblies with pocket numbers and measured lengths"; "Tool wear and life | … | 4". ISO 13399-1:2006 was last confirmed in 2021 (https://www.iso.org/standard/36757.html).
**Fix:** Phase 1 importers (tool context): ISO 13399 Part 21 data inside vendor catalog packages, DIN 4000 property mapping, and the documented tool-library formats of the most common incumbent CAM systems [unverified which are documented]; presetter readings (length, radius, runout) as signed External inputs keyed by tool-assembly serial. Holders and extensions are full collision Bodies. Per-machine tool tables map tool Assemblies to T number, pocket and H and D registers, and posts read them. Count-based tool life (minutes or parts per edge) moves to phase 1; model-based life stays in phase 4. Oracle: a vendor package round trip with geometry within 1 µm and properties unchanged; conflicting tool-table entries fail the build.

**Section:** KLN Items and item numbers, Change management; MFG Approval and machine safety, MBOM and routings.
**Problem:** Every NC program, routing or work-instruction change goes through the engineering release path, but shops change programs daily (feeds, step-downs, a better tool) without touching the part definition. Without a manufacturing change lane with its own revisions and approvers, either engineering change control drowns in shop edits or programmers bypass it.
**Evidence:** MFG: "The release is a signed tag in `repo`. Released programs are immutable artifacts in CAS."; KLN Item kinds are "`Part`, `Assembly`, `Document`, `Software`, `Purchased`"; KLN's change-order sequence has no manufacturing-only variant.
**Fix:** KLN adds a manufacturing change order (MCO) policy class: scope limited to MBOM, routings, programs, fixtures, work instructions and inspection plans; a check rejects any change to an EBOM Item definition; approvers are manufacturing roles; programs and routings carry their own revision sequence and effectivity by work order or lot, with states `Prototype` (first-article run under a deviation), `Proven` (after a passing first-article record) and `Released`. Add Item kind `Program`. MFG step 4 becomes "release through an MCO". Oracle: an MCO touching an EBOM definition is rejected; an ECO changing a part invalidates exactly the dependent programs.

**Section:** Phasing in each tab.
**Problem:** The GP1 chain is phased inconsistently. MEC title blocks read item and revision from `repo` and drawings carry BOM tables in phase 1, MFG rolls up BOM cost and releases programs in phase 1, and UIX's phase-1 gate approves GP1 through the UI; but KLN delivers Items, revisions and BOM views in phase 2, UIX delivers toolpath playback and the cost panel in phase 2, chamfer and deburr toolpaths (needed for edge breaks on any machined part) are phase 2, and AGT's CAM programmer role is phase 2 while MFG ships agent-proposed toolpaths in phase 1.
**Evidence:** KLN phasing: "2 Mechanical depth | … | … Items, revisions, change orders …; EBOM, MBOM and SBOM views". MEC: "Sheets and title blocks | … read item, revision and approvals from `repo` | 1"; "Tables | BOM … | 1 (BOM, holes), 2". MFG: "BOM roll-up | `repo` BOM query … | 1"; "Deburr and chamfer | … | 2"; agent-proposed toolpaths "Phase 1". UIX: "Toolpath playback | … | 2"; "Cost panel | … | 2". AGT role catalog: CAM programmer, phase 2.
**Fix:** KLN phase 1 adds a minimal lifecycle: item numbers, revision labels on release tags, `InWork` and `Released` states and the EBOM view; full change orders, effectivity and MBOM stay in phase 2. UIX moves toolpath playback, the NC view (R4-06) and the cost panel to phase 1. MFG moves 2D chamfer and edge-break toolpaths to phase 1. AGT moves the CAM programmer role to phase 1, or MFG moves agent proposals to phase 2; state the same choice in both tabs. KLN either delivers the interchangeability check with change orders in phase 2 or states that phase-2 change orders take a human verdict.

**Section:** Process categories; Printer profiles, 3MF and machine connectivity; Phasing.
**Problem:** The phase-1 wedge assumes Crucible's own FFF slicer drives printers through OctoPrint, Moonraker and PrusaLink. The slicers people use carry years of printer and filament profiles, and the most common professional desktop printers impose formats and access rules the spec ignores: Bambu Lab firmware routes third-party control through Bambu Connect, also in LAN mode, and Prusa's binary G-code has an AGPL reference library.
**Evidence:** MFG: "Material extrusion | FFF … | G-code (Marlin, Klipper, RepRapFirmware flavors)"; "Printer connectivity | Send, start, pause, cancel, monitor … | 1". Bambu Lab, 16 January 2025: Bambu Connect "removes slicing functions while enabling remote control and print initiation", and the restrictions apply in LAN mode (https://blog.bambulab.com/firmware-update-introducing-new-authorization-control-system-2/). libbgcode is AGPL-3.0 (https://github.com/prusa3d/libbgcode).
**Fix:** The phase-1 default for FFF is slicer hand-off: write a 3MF build with plates, per-object orientation, modifiers and settings in the metadata that OrcaSlicer, Bambu Studio and PrusaSlicer read [unverified per slicer], and open it in the user's slicer. Crucible's native slicer stays for what only it does (direct slicing of implicit lattices for GP2, Field-driven infill) and becomes the default only after matching the reference slicers on the stated thin-wall corpus and on print time. Write bgcode from the published format description, never linking libbgcode. Reach Bambu printers only through the vendor's sanctioned path and say so. Printer start follows R4-01.

**Section:** MFG Inspection planning and CMM programming, First-article inspection and PPAP; MEC Drawings.
**Problem:** MEC drawings have item balloons tied to BOM lines but no characteristic balloons, and D-MFG-18 rejects balloon numbers as identity without saying where printed balloon numbers come from, how they stay stable across revisions, and how Form 3 rows match them. Job shops, the GP1 audience, mostly inspect against customer PDF drawings with no Crucible model, and D-MFG-18 extracts characteristics only from native GD&T.
**Evidence:** MEC: "balloons tied to BOM items". MFG D-MFG-18: "*Rejected:* balloon numbers as identity"; "Characteristic extraction | Design -> characteristics … with balloons | … | 2". IAQG's summary of 9102 revision C adds definitions for "Ballooned Design Characteristic" and "Ballooned Document" (https://ma.iaqg.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/10/9102_Changes_07112023.pdf).
**Fix:** MEC adds a characteristic-balloon annotation kind bound to D-MFG-18 identities. Labels are allocated once per identity, never reused, kept for unchanged characteristics across revisions and renumbered only by explicit command; each release produces the ballooned PDF that Form 3, inspection plans and reports cite. MFG adds a foreign-drawing workflow in phase 2: import a customer PDF as a controlled document, place balloons by hand or through an agent extraction Proposal with page coordinates, and create typed characteristics (nominal, limits, feature type) linked to the customer STEP when present. Oracle: a revision that changes one dimension changes one balloon's content and no labels; Form 3 rows equal the balloon set.

**Section:** First-article inspection and PPAP; Statistical process control.
**Problem:** The PPAP row lists an unverified partial element set, omits submission levels and has no measurement system analysis, which PPAP requires and which method selection needs. PFMEA names no method, although automotive customers expect the AIAG and VDA approach.
**Evidence:** MFG: "PPAP | Submission package with process flow …, PFMEA and control plan links, MSA, dimensional results, capability studies, material results and the part submission warrant [unverified for element list]"; SPC covers control charts and capability only. AIAG lists PPAP 4th edition as current (https://www.aiag.org/training-and-resources/manuals/details/PPAP-4). The AIAG and VDA FMEA Handbook is in its first edition, second printing, with a 7-step PFMEA approach (https://www.aiag.org/training-and-resources/manuals/details/FMEAAV-1).
**Fix:** Model PPAP as a data package for the 4th edition: the element list (design records, engineering change documents, customer engineering approval, DFMEA, process flow, PFMEA, control plan, MSA studies, dimensional results, material and performance test records, initial process studies, qualified laboratory documentation, appearance approval report, sample parts, master sample, checking aids, customer-specific requirements, part submission warrant) and the level 1 to 5 retention matrix, with customer-specific overlays. Add MSA to SPC in phase 3: gauge R&R by average and range and by ANOVA, bias, linearity, stability and attribute agreement, with study records linked to gauges and characteristics; method selection reads the measured %GRR. PFMEA and DFMEA follow the handbook's 7-step structure with action priority, DFMEA linked to MEC checks. Customer special-characteristic symbols are data.

**Section:** MEC Drawings; KLN Revisions and lifecycle states; UIX Drawings and model-based definition.
**Problem:** Drawings get a revision table but no revision markers. Practitioners flag each changed item with a revision symbol or cloud and list the change by zone; Crucible has the semantic diff to generate them, but no tab specifies it. Tabulated drawings, the usual way to document dash-number families, are also missing.
**Evidence:** MEC: "Tables | … revisions (from `repo` releases and change orders) …"; no tab specifies revision clouds, revision symbols or tabulated drawings. ASME lists Y14.35-2025 as the current edition of the revision standard (https://www.asme.org/codes-standards/find-codes-standards/y14-35-revision-engineering-drawings-associated-documents).
**Fix:** MEC adds `revision_markers(drawing, from: Release, to: Release, style: Delta | Cloud)`: the annotation and view diff between two releases places a symbol beside each changed item, fills the revision block with change-order number, description and zone, and regenerates at release. Markers and revision text are late-bound release fields excluded from the definition digest (R4-17). Drafting packages carry Y14.35-2025 rules and the ISO practice. Add tabulated drawings driven by `family` rows. Released drawings are also written as PDF/A [unverified part] for archive. Oracle: a release changing two dimensions yields exactly two markers and one revision row.

**Section:** KLN Revisions and lifecycle states (D-KLN-26); Keys and behavior versions.
**Problem:** "Modified since release" compares evaluated `ItemDefinition`s, which include B-rep `ObjectId`s and controlled documents, so an engine or std upgrade that changes bits within tolerance, or a drafting-package update that re-renders PDFs, marks every released Item modified: the noise D-KLN-26 exists to remove. The rule is also circular wherever revision text is part of the content: title blocks, silkscreen revision marks and engraved part markings change when the revision is assigned.
**Evidence:** KLN: "The `ItemDefinition` record holds the canonical evaluated Part or Assembly `ObjectId`, …, the product manufacturing information (PMI), properties and controlled documents."; "Upgrading versions is an explicit Proposal that shows the geometric and metric diff". MEC title blocks "read item, revision and approvals from `repo`".
**Fix:** Define a definition digest separate from storage identity: geometry compared by topology plus per-face equality within a declared definition tolerance (default the smaller of 0.1 µm and 1% of the tightest tolerance on the Item), PMI, properties and BOM by value, documents by semantic content (views, annotation items, notes), never PDF bytes. Lifecycle-bound text (revision label, release date, approvers, serials) is a late-bound placeholder filled at output time and excluded from the digest; ELX silkscreen revision text and MEC `emboss` markings use the same placeholder. Upgrade Proposals classify each Item as unchanged, document-only or substantive. Oracle: an engine upgrade with bit-level changes only flips zero Items to modified.

**Section:** KLN BOM views, Events and webhooks; MFG Machine and MES connectivity, MBOM and routings.
**Problem:** ERP integration is one sentence: a webhook consumer that reads change notices and BOM views. Real integration is bidirectional and field-mapped: item master, multi-level BOM with reference designators and effectivity, routings with work centers and standard times, and change notices with stock disposition go out; standard cost, purchase price, lead time and on-hand inventory come back for cost models and dispositions. MES integration is phase 4 with no information model.
**Evidence:** KLN: "The ERP connector is a standard webhook consumer: it reads change notices and BOM views and posts acknowledgements back as lifecycle records."; KLN EBOM lists find numbers but no reference designators; MFG: "MES integration | Work orders, routings, routing-step status, scrap and labor bookings over OPC UA or REST plugins | … | 4".
**Fix:** ECO specifies an `io/erp` connector world (tool context) with mappings as Ingot data: outbound `ItemMaster`, `BillOfMaterials` (find number, quantity with unit, reference designators, effectivity, phantom flag, substitute groups), `Routing` (operation sequence, work center, setup and run time, tooling) and `ChangeNotice` (effectivity, disposition per stock location); inbound External inputs for costs, prices, lead times and inventory. Messages follow OAGIS business object documents for ERP and ISA-95 (IEC 62264) B2MML for MES [unverified current versions]; reference connectors for one large ERP and one open-source ERP in phase 2. A field-ownership table states which system owns each field. KLN adds reference designators to EBOM lines. Oracle: round trip against a mock ERP with idempotent replay of every event.

**Section:** KLN Product lifecycle management; ECO Migration from incumbent tools (Tooling for switching teams).
**Problem:** Crucible assumes it is the system of record for item numbers, revisions, change orders and BOMs. Most manufacturers that would adopt it keep an enterprise PLM or PDM authoritative for years and exchange with suppliers through it, but there is no subordinate mode: no external numbering, no import of external approvals and no publication of releases into the external vault before phase 4.
**Evidence:** KLN: "PLM in Crucible is not a separate vault."; numbering policy is internal. ECO: "PDM history | … | Licensed PDM connectors or exported revision sets | 4"; "Parallel run" and "Round-trip bridge" (phase 3) re-import releases rather than publish them.
**Fix:** KLN adds a system-of-record policy per record type (item number, revision label, lifecycle state, change order, BOM, approvals) with values `Crucible` or `External(connector)`. With `External`, numbers are allocated through the connector, Crucible's release Act publishes a release package (AP242 with PMI, PDF drawings, BOM, NC programs, and an Ingot source archive with its digest) into the external item revision, and external approvals return as signed External inputs whose payload names the Crucible content digest, so D-KLN-28 still binds approval to content. ECO ships connectors for two enterprise PLM systems and one cloud PLM in phase 2 [unverified API names]. Oracle: against a mock PLM, a Crucible release and an external approval round trip without changing digests.

**Section:** ELX Catalog-part selection (D-ELX-3), Creating catalog parts; MEC Standard parts and fasteners; KLN Items and item numbers.
**Problem:** Parametric selection resolves against the open catalog to a manufacturer part number and `fasten` picks the shortest standard length, but companies design with internal part numbers from an approved parts list whose approved-manufacturer list carries alternates, and component engineering controls what may be used. ELX never references KLN's `Purchased` Items, so the design BOM, the ERP BOM and the assembly house's BOM disagree.
**Evidence:** ELX D-ELX-3: "A circuit element names either an exact catalog part or a parametric selection, which is a `Query` over the catalog."; MEC: `fasten` "picks the shortest standard length that satisfies both"; KLN: "`approved_sources` | For `Purchased`: catalog part references with manufacturer part numbers, ranked"; ELX contains no "IPN", "AVL" or "AML".
**Fix:** Add an organization parts-policy package: approved internal part numbers (`Purchased` Items) with approved manufacturers, lifecycle (preliminary, approved, not recommended, obsolete) and preferred flags. ELX elements and MEC fasteners may name an internal number; parametric selections and `fasten` resolve over approved parts first and reach the open catalog only with a recorded waiver; BOM views list internal number plus approved manufacturers, and supplier snapshots attach per manufacturer part. Component engineering is a Proposal workflow: a new-part request creates the internal number, catalog facets and approved manufacturers in one reviewable change. Oracle: a design using a non-approved part fails the policy check unless a waiver names it.

**Section:** ELX Variants (D-ELX-4); KLN Variants and the 150% BOM (D-KLN-27).
**Problem:** ELX models a variant as one enum value and builds every declared variant in CI, while KLN models options with rules and rejects enumeration as exponential; a product with region, feature-level and assembly options cannot follow both. ELX also lets a variant pick different parts, possibly with different footprints, so copper can differ between assembly variants with no check, although the bare board must be one fabricated item.
**Evidence:** ELX: "A variant is a value of the design's `Variant` parameter"; `match variant { Variant.eu => parts::nordic::nrf9161(), _ => parts::nordic::nrf9151() }`; "Every declared variant builds and passes its checks in CI." KLN D-KLN-27: "*Rejected:* … enumerating configurations (exponential in the number of options)."
**Fix:** ELX adopts the contract's record-of-options form with KLN's semantics; CI builds the declared sellable configurations plus a pairwise covering set and evaluates the rest symbolically. Add check `bare_board_invariant`: copper, drill, outline, mask and silkscreen of a bare-board Part are identical across assembly variants unless a fabrication variant is declared with its own bare-board Item. Variant alternates share a land pattern or use a declared multi-footprint land pattern. Per-variant outputs state paste handling for unfitted parts (kept, or a declared variant stencil). Oracle: a seeded variant that changes a footprint fails the invariant check.

**Section:** ELX Writing a circuit (schematic module and editor behavior); Electrical rule checks.
**Problem:** The stored drawing models pin-to-pin wires only, so real schematics cannot be stored: wires meeting wires at junctions, power symbols, no-connect flags, bus entries, sheet symbols. Nothing stops the drawing from lying: a code edit can leave a drawn wire between pins that are no longer connected, and only removed pins are caught. Labels are drawing items, although in every schematic tool a label is connectivity, and net ties (an intended short at one point) have no representation although IPC-2581C carries intended net shorts.
**Evidence:** ELX: `wire w_3c1 [u1.pin("SW"), l1.a] path [(78mm, 40mm)]`; "A wire end that touches no pin is impossible: the editor snaps or refuses."; "Annotations that point at removed pins fail with `SchematicError::StaleAnnotation`"; ELX contains no schematic junction or "net tie". MFG cites IPC-2581C support for "intended net shorts".
**Fix:** The `Schematic` module stores drawn topology: segments whose ends lie on pins, labels, power symbols, sheet pins or other segments (explicit junctions), plus no-connect flags and bus entries. A blocking check `schematic_matches_circuit` maps each drawn connected group to exactly one net; a group spanning two nets is `SchematicError::DrawnShort`, drawn in the danger style and failing release. Label text equals the net name: editing it renames the net in source, and placing a label with an existing net's name writes a `connect`. Net ties are explicit `tie(net_a, net_b, at: footprint)` elements that ERC, DRC, netlists and IPC-2581 export treat as intended shorts; no-connect flags write `no_connect(pin)`. Oracle: the 10⁵-edit property test also asserts that no drawn group spans two nets after any code edit.

**Section:** Circuit simulation (Engine choice, Netlist and model import); State of the art.
**Problem:** Board designers judge a simulator by whether vendor models run. Many regulator and amplifier models ship encrypted for PSpice or LTspice [unverified share] or use dialect features a new engine will lack for years, and the spec only lists them as unsupported. The headline metric is C6288 runtime against VACASK, which says nothing about vendor-model coverage.
**Evidence:** ELX: "Unsupported constructs, such as an encrypted PSpice model, are listed with their file and line and never skipped silently."; "A design may select `engine: ngspice` for one analysis explicitly"; target "C6288 benchmark with PSP103.4 models: within 1.2× of VACASK's runtime". ngspice's news page records PSpice and LTspice compatibility work across several releases (https://ngspice.sourceforge.io/news.html).
**Fix:** In phase 3, imported vendor models run by default in ngspice as an External Op labelled with its host; the native engine runs native and Verilog-A models, Monte Carlo and adjoints, and a vendor model moves to it only after matching ngspice on its own test bench. Offer LTspice and PSpice as optional External Ops where the user holds a licence [unverified batch-mode terms] for encrypted models, and state plainly that encrypted models never run in the native engine. Make the primary metric a vendor-model corpus (regulators, op-amps, MOSFETs and gate drivers from at least five vendors): the share that parse, converge and match the vendor's reference engine within 1% on the vendor's test circuit, target 95% of unencrypted models.

**Section:** ELX Panelization, Fabrication and assembly outputs, DFM, DFA and test for assembled boards; MFG Electronics manufacturing handoff.
**Problem:** Both tabs specify panelization, fabrication and assembly outputs and the same DFM and DFA check families, with different decisions and versions: MFG makes IPC-2581C primary and cites Gerber revision 2024.05, ELX lists Gerber first and cites 2026.05; MFG puts test programs in phase 4, ELX test checks in phase 3. Two teams will build two panelizers and two rule sets.
**Evidence:** MFG: "Panelization | Boards -> panel with rails, tabs …" and "Fab DFM | Annular ring, trace and space …" (phase 3); "Ucamco's current Gerber specification is revision 2024.05". ELX: "Panelization | Panel Assembly with breakaways and coupons" (phase 3); DFM check-family table; "Gerber X2 | Gerber Layer Format Specification, revision 2026.05". Ucamco lists revision 2026.05, dated 19 May 2026, as the latest layer specification (https://www.ucamco.com/en/gerber/downloads).
**Fix:** Assign ownership once: MFG owns capability records, fabricator and assembler rule packs, panelization, stencil design and output writers; ELX owns the DRC engine, board-side check presentation and the board data writers read, and replaces its duplicate tables with one-line pointers. Update MFG to Gerber revision 2026.05 and state the primary-format decision once, in MFG. Put test-point checks and test-program outputs in one phase (phase 3, because GP5 is assembled then).

**Section:** ELX Design rules and the constraint manager, DFM, DFA and test; MFG Electronics manufacturing handoff.
**Problem:** The board-house vocabulary is missing: IPC-6012 performance classes (which change annular ring, plating and acceptance rules), IPC-A-600 and IPC-A-610 acceptability, J-STD-001 soldering requirements, IPC-4101 laminate designations on the stackup, IPC-2152 trace current capacity, and fabrication-drawing notes that state these. There is also no feature to add test points (pad, probe side, fixture keepouts), only a coverage check.
**Evidence:** No draft mentions "IPC-6012", "IPC-A-600", "IPC-A-610", "J-STD-001", "IPC-4101" or "IPC-2152"; ELX DFM table: "Test | Test-point coverage per net, probe spacing, fixture side, boundary-scan chain integrity". IPC lists IPC-6012E as the qualification and performance specification for rigid printed boards (https://shop.electronics.org/ipc-6012/ipc-6012-standard-only/Revision-e/english).
**Fix:** Add board-level `fab_class` and `assembly_class` (Class 2, 3, 3/A) that select rule packs in MFG capability data (annular ring and breakout, plating thickness, acceptability references), with revisions pinned in licensed data packages. Stackup materials carry IPC-4101 designations. A fabrication-drawing generator writes class, material, finish, impedance tolerance and acceptance notes from these values. Add an IPC-2152-based current-capacity screen beside IR drop. Add `test_point` features (pad style, side, minimum pitch, keepout height) and an automatic test-point Proposal for nets without access. Phase 3.

**Section:** Design rules and the constraint manager; Pack design (Safety).
**Problem:** Creepage and clearance come from voltage, pollution degree and material group under IEC 60664-1, but a product is judged against its end-product safety standard (for example IEC 62368-1, IEC 61010-1 or IEC 60601-1), whose tables, insulation grades and working-voltage rules differ. A rule without insulation grade, overvoltage category, peak or RMS working voltage, altitude and slot treatment gives wrong spacing on safety-critical boards.
**Evidence:** ELX: `clearance(class("hv_400v"), all) >= creepage(400V, pollution: 2, group: IIIa)`; pack safety: "insulation coordination, creepage and clearance by voltage and pollution degree under IEC 60664-1 [unverified edition]".
**Fix:** Change the constructors to `creepage(standard: SafetyStandard, insulation: Functional | Basic | Supplementary | Reinforced, working_voltage: { peak, rms }, ovc: Ovc, pollution: Pd, material_group: Mg, altitude: Length)` and the same for clearance, with tables as licensed data packages per standard edition and a required declaration of the standard for each isolation barrier. Results carry the screening label, list the barriers checked, and apply slot and coating rules only as the chosen standard permits. Oracle: worked examples from each supported standard.

**Section:** MFG D-MFG-16; ELX Fabrication and assembly outputs, Open questions 1; ECO Electronics.
**Problem:** Three tabs take three ODB++ positions (licensed plugin only; phase 4 after a partnership; build after a format agreement), and their shared premise is out of date: an open-source tool now writes ODB++. Many fabricators' CAM front ends take ODB++ as their main input [unverified share], so deferring it to phase 4 weakens GP5's "outputs alone" gate at real board houses.
**Evidence:** MFG: "ODB++ is available only through a licensed translator plugin."; ELX: "ODB++ | ODB++ version 8.1 | … | 4 (needs format partnership, see Open questions)"; ECO: "Build, after a format agreement with the owner (ELX open question) | 4". KiCad 9.0 release notes list "ODB++ export" (https://www.kicad.org/blog/2025/02/Version-9.0.0-Released/).
**Fix:** Close ELX open question 1: treat ODB++ as a published vendor specification that open-source tools write, check Siemens' current terms once, and Build an own writer in phase 3 beside IPC-2581C and Gerber, with KiCad's writer as an external differential oracle (never linked, since KiCad is GPL). Rewrite D-MFG-16's last sentence and align ECO's row.

**Section:** ECO Migration from incumbent tools, Formats not supported; ELX Creating catalog parts.
**Problem:** Migration covers mechanical CAD only. There is no path for EAGLE, Altium, EasyEDA, CADSTAR or OrCAD designs and libraries, although Autodesk stopped selling and supporting EAGLE on 7 June 2026 and KiCad 9 already imports several of these formats. ELX limits proprietary libraries to licensed translators that do not exist for most ECAD formats, and IPC-2581 is read only for fabricator feedback, so legacy boards without schematics cannot even be re-spun.
**Evidence:** ECO "What can move" has MCAD rows only; ELX: "Proprietary library formats come only through licensed translator plugins"; ECO IPC-2581: "W; R of fabricator feedback". Autodesk: "Effective June 7, 2026, Autodesk will no longer sell or support EAGLE." (https://www.autodesk.com/products/fusion-360/blog/future-of-autodesk-eagle-fusion-360-electronics/). KiCad 9 imports EAGLE 6.x or newer XML, CADSTAR, EasyEDA, Altium SchDoc and PcbDoc, P-CAD and Fabmaster files (https://docs.kicad.org/9.0/en/kicad/kicad.html).
**Fix:** Add ECAD rows to "What can move" in phase 3: EAGLE XML schematics, boards and libraries by a Build importer; Altium, CADSTAR, EasyEDA, P-CAD and Fabmaster through KiCad's importers run as an external tool in a pinned container (GPL code may run outside the process), then Crucible's KiCad importer; IPC-2581 and ODB++ read of legacy boards as layout, netlist and BOM; library migration of symbols, footprints and parameters to catalog parts and internal numbers (R4-20). Oracles: netlist equality with the source tool's own netlist export; Gerber XOR against the source tool's outputs.

**Section:** ECO Electronics; ELX IDX V6 for external tools; MEC Phasing.
